### Reviewer 3

This work involves wet treatment of the cathode material with sodium persulfate to pre-oxidize Ni in the cathode, facilitating
subsequent solid-state sintering regeneration. Although the overall drawing level is relatively high, the innovation of the
research is average, lacking a comparison of advantages with the traditional solid-state lithium replenishment process,
such as lithium diffusion kinetics. Moreover, from an environmental perspective, this paper lacks an environmental
economic analysis, which raises doubts about the use of persulfate.
1. The manuscript lacks a quantitative comparison of Li⁺ diffusion kinetics during solid-state sintering between pre-oxidized
and conventional regeneration routes. It remains unclear whether the pre-oxidation strategy genuinely enhances Li+
transport kinetics or reduces Li salt consumption in subsequent sintering. Quantitative metrics, such as Li+ diffusion
coefficients, activation energies, or Li salt utilization efficiency, should be provided to substantiate the claimed kinetic
advantages of pre-oxidation over traditional methods.
2. While direct regeneration is positioned as an eco-friendly alternative to pyro-/hydro-metallurgy, the environmental footprint
of the pre-oxidation step (using substantial Na2S2O8) remains unaddressed. A life-cycle assessment comparing carbon
emissions, energy consumption, and upstream chemical production impacts between this strategy and existing recycling
methods is essential. Furthermore, economic viability metrics (e.g., reagent cost per ton of regenerated cathode) are absent,
undermining the practical relevance of the proposed approach.
3. Wastewater management from Na2S2O8 rinsing and potential SO2 emissions during high-temperature calcination (due to
sulfate residues) are not discussed. Residual sodium ions may degrade electrochemical performance, yet no data on Na
content in regenerated materials (e.g., ICP analysis) is provided. Clarification is needed on: (1) wastewater treatment
protocols, (2) measures to suppress SO2 release, and (3) quantification of impurity retention (Na/S) and their effects on
cycling stability.
4. The schematic in Fig. 2c lacks a corresponding description in the main text or caption. This figure illustrates structural
evolution from NiO rock-salt to layered NiOOH/LiNiO2 but omits labels for atomic rearrangements or stress-induced
fragmentation. Enhanced annotation is required to align the visual with the proposed
mechanism.

General Comment: This research introduces an innovative pre-oxidation strategy for
directly regenerating spent NCM cathode materials. The authors achieve surface-to-
bulk Li+ diffusion channel restoration by converting surface inert NiO to layered
NiOOH and reducing Li+/Ni2+ mixing by oxidizing the anti-site Ni2+ in the bulk phase
to Ni3+ via the one-pot pre-oxidation treatment. I find that the engineering is very good
which not only facilitates the decomposition of secondary particles into primary
particles, enabling subsequent homogeneous re-lithiation, but also facilitates the
coalescence of particles in subsequent calcination, enabling the formation of large
single-crystal. As a result, the regenerated single-crystal NCM achieves a high tap
density along with excellent electrochemical performance. In my opinion, the article
meets the standards of Nature Communications and can be accepted for publication
after minor revisions.
Overall Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the positive comments,
particularly the remarks that “the engineering is very good” and “the regenerated single-
crystal NCM achieves a high tap density and excellent electrochemical performance”.
Indeed, as the reviewer commented, our pre-oxidation strategy effectively transforms
the surface NiO into layered NiOOH and oxidizes anti-site Ni2+ in the bulk into Ni3+,
thereby reconstructing the Li+ diffusion channels from the surface to the bulk. The
oxidation-induced structural transitions facilitate the decomposition of secondary
particles into primary particles, enabling homogeneous re-lithiation. These synergistic
processes collectively enable the restoration of structural order and morphological
uniformity, which are essential for achieving high-performance regeneration.
In the response, we have supplemented experimental data and comprehensive
analyses to further elucidate the oxidation mechanism. We believe these experimental
results and extended discussions can well address your concerns. We hope these efforts
can further solidify the foundation of the pre-oxidation strategy and provide clarity on
the scientific contributions of our research.
1. The study demonstrates that a one-hour oxidation treatment of spent NCM523
effectively transforms the NiO rock-salt phase into layered NiOOH while
simultaneously oxidizing Ni2+ to Ni3+. Why is one-hour? Experimental data for shorter
oxidation times should be supplemented to improve the reliability of the oxidation
experiment.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful question. In this study, various
oxidation durations are systematically investigated, and the one-hour condition is
selected as the optimized treatment to present the best results. To address the reviewer’s
concern, we have included data for the 0.5-hour oxidation treatment to improve the
completeness and reliability of the analysis.
As shown in Fig. R1 and Table R1, XRD refinement indicates that although the
0.5-hour treatment removes the NiO rock-salt phase, the Li+/Ni2+ mixing remains
higher (5.67%) than that of the 1-hour sample (4.59%). Consistently, ICP analysis
(Table R2) shows a Li/TM ratio of 0.47 for the 0.5-hour sample, compared with 0.45
for the 1- and 6-hour ones. These results suggest that shorter oxidation time leads to
incomplete oxidation of anti-site Ni2+. In contrast, oxidation for ≥1 hour ensures
sufficient Ni2+→Ni3+ conversion, confirming that a 1-hour treatment is essential for
achieving material reconstruction.
